title: Buffer Solutions and Titrations - Chemistry - Acid–Base Titrations
subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In a titration, what is the difference between the **equivalence point** and the **end point**?
options: They are identical terms for the same moment.
The equivalence point is determined geometrically, while the end point is calculated stoichiometrically.
The equivalence point is the stoichiometric point where moles of acid equals moles of base; the end point is the visible color change of the indicator.
The equivalence point always occurs at pH 7, whereas the end point depends on the indicator.
questions.explain: The equivalence point is the theoretical point where the titrant has exactly reacted with the analyte in stoichiometric proportions. The end point is the experimental point where the indicator changes color. Ideally, these points are close, but they are conceptually distinct.

questions.q: What is a **standard solution** in the context of titration?
options: A solution that always has a pH of 7.
A solution of accurately known concentration used to determine the concentration of an unknown.
A buffer solution used to calibrate pH meters.
questions.explain: A standard solution is a solution containing a known concentration of an element or substance. In titrations, it is the titrant used to react with the analyte to determine its concentration.

questions.q: What volume of $$ 0.200\,\text{M} $$ NaOH is required to exactly neutralize $$ 25.0\,\text{mL} $$ of $$ 0.100\,\text{M} $$ HCl?
questions.explain:
Using $$ M_a V_a = M_b V_b $$ (since stoichiometry is 1:1): 
$$ (0.100\,\text{M})(25.0\,\text{mL}) = (0.200\,\text{M})(V_b) $$ 
$$ 2.50 = 0.200 V_b $$ 
$$ V_b = 12.5\,\text{mL} $$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: When titrating a diprotic weak acid (like $$ \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 $$) with a strong base, how many distinct equivalence points are theoretically observable on the titration curve?
questions.explain: A diprotic acid has two ionizable protons. Titration with a strong base will show two stepwise neutralization reactions, resulting in two distinct equivalence points (provided the $$ K_a $$ values are sufficiently different).
